introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde et questions 1 à 12) ; filigranes gcerevision ignorés. Le texte de la page 2 transparaît en miroir sur la page de garde (verso mal opacifié) et quelques espaces sont manquants à l'impression (question 8 : « between1871and1890 », rétabli en « between 1871 and 1890 ») ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune citation n'est inventée et les chiffres sont limités à des repères datés de l'historiographie courante (dates, traités) ; à relire par un historien avant mise en vente.

Question 4 : l'énoncé imprimé date le déclenchement de la révolte Mau Mau de 1951. L'historiographie situe la montée de la violence en 1950-52 (mouvement interdit en août 1950, état d'urgence proclamé le 20 octobre 1952) ; le sujet est recopié tel quel et le corrigé précise la chronologie sans corriger l'énoncé.

Question 5 : l'Afrique équatoriale française regroupe le Gabon, le Moyen-Congo, l'Oubangui-Chari et le Tchad ; le Cameroun, ancien mandat puis tutelle, n'en faisait pas partie. Les interventions militaires françaises (Gabon 1964, Tchad à partir de la fin des années 1960, Centrafrique 1979) et le rôle du réseau Foccart sont cités selon l'historiographie courante, sans chiffres.

Question 7 : le sujet emploie « romanisation » au sens de la promotion du catholicisme romain par Jacques II ; les dates de 1688 sont données en style ancien (naissance du prince le 10 juin, acquittement des sept évêques et invitation à Guillaume le 30 juin, débarquement à Torbay le 5 novembre).

Question 9 : le montant des réparations (132 milliards de marks-or, fixé en 1921) et les pertes territoriales sont cités de mémoire historique établie ; aucune statistique de population n'est avancée.

Question 11 : la Banque mondiale et le FMI sont des institutions spécialisées de l'ONU ; l'UNICEF (fonds et non institution spécialisée) n'est volontairement pas traité. Les dates (variole déclarée éradiquée en 1980, Alma-Ata 1978, convention 182 de l'OIT en 1999, Codex Alimentarius 1963, retrait des États-Unis de l'UNESCO en 1984-85) sont citées selon l'historiographie courante.

Question 12 : le sujet vise la rupture sino-soviétique après la mort de Staline (1953). Les dates (discours de Khrouchtchev en février 1956, rupture de l'accord nucléaire en 1959, retrait des conseillers en 1960, congrès de Bucarest en juin 1960, guerre sino-indienne 1962, incidents de l'Oussouri en mars 1969) sont données selon l'historiographie courante ; aucun chiffre n'est avancé.

Thèmes : les noms sont qualifiés pour éviter les collisions avec les Tags de l'Histoire francophone (`sino-soviet split`, `afrikaner nationalism`, `mau mau revolt in kenya`...) ; plusieurs sont réutilisés des sujets History 2020-2021 (`scramble for africa`, `apartheid in south africa`, `cold war`, `indirect rule in colonial africa`) ; à revérifier à l'ingestion avec `find_tag_variant`.

questions.enonce_markdown:
To what extent did the romanisation policies of James II influence the English Revolution?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The English (or "Glorious") Revolution of 1688-89 removed the Catholic king James II (James VII of Scotland) and placed his Protestant daughter Mary and her Dutch husband William of Orange on the throne, on terms that confirmed the powers of Parliament in the Bill of Rights (1689). "Romanisation" here means James's policy of promoting the Roman Catholic faith and Catholics in the Protestant kingdom of England. The question asks how far this policy caused the revolution. It is argued here that it was the main cause, because it united Whigs, Tories and the Church of England against the king, but that it worked together with James's absolutist methods, the birth of a Catholic heir and the intervention of William of Orange.

**1. James II's Catholic policies.**
- James, who had converted to Catholicism before he became king (his refusal to take the Anglican sacrament under the Test Act led to his resignation as Lord High Admiral in 1673), came to the throne in 1685 with Parliament's support after Charles II's death and the defeat of Monmouth's rebellion (1685), so many Protestants first accepted that his Catholicism would be temporary, since his heirs, Mary and Anne, were Protestants.
- *The army and offices.* He built up a larger standing army and gave commissions to Catholic officers against the Test Act (1673). In *Godden v Hales* (1686) judges supported his claim to a dispensing power, that is the right to excuse individuals from the law, and Catholics were appointed to the Privy Council, the universities, local government and the Irish army (where the Earl of Tyrconnell replaced Protestants with Catholics).
- *The Church of England.* The Court of Ecclesiastical Commission (1686) was used to discipline the Church; the Bishop of London, Henry Compton, was suspended for refusing to dismiss a preacher who criticised Catholicism, and in 1687 James forced Catholic fellows into Magdalen College, Oxford, which angered the Anglican establishment.
- *Declarations of Indulgence.* In April 1687 James issued a Declaration of Indulgence suspending the penal laws against Catholics and Protestant dissenters, and a second declaration in April 1688 ordered that it be read in all churches. Seven bishops, led by Archbishop Sancroft, petitioned against reading it; they were tried for seditious libel and acquitted on 30 June 1688 to widespread rejoicing.
- *Remodelling of Parliament.* James tried to pack a Parliament that would repeal the Test Act and penal laws by changing the town corporations and officials, and thus attacked the traditional position of the Tory gentry, who had been his main support.

**2. How these policies caused the revolution.**
- They destroyed the alliance of Anglican Tories, who believed in non-resistance, and the Whigs, who had always opposed him. Once the Church itself was attacked, the Tories were willing to consider resistance.
- The birth of James's son, James Francis Edward, on 10 June 1688 meant that there would now be a Catholic heir instead of Protestant Mary, so Catholic rule might become permanent. The next month, on 30 June 1688, seven leading figures (the "Immortal Seven": Danby, Shrewsbury, Devonshire, Lumley, Compton, Russell and Sidney) invited William to come to England.
- The use of the army and the dispensing power also frightened people about English liberties, which connected religion with the constitution.

**3. Other factors.**
- *Absolutism.* The king's use of the dispensing and suspending powers, his treatment of the judges, and his attempt to control Parliament seemed to put him above the law, in the manner of Louis XIV. The Revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685 and the flight of French Huguenots to England made English Protestants fear that Catholic absolutism would come to England as well.
- *William's own aims.* William was the leader of the Dutch resistance to Louis XIV and wished to bring England on to the side of the anti-French coalition. His landing at Torbay on 5 November 1688 with a large army was a Dutch military operation as much as a response to the invitation, and James's army and supporters (including John Churchill) deserted him, so James fled in December 1688.
- *Political miscalculation.* James moved too quickly, did not give the policy time to work, and ignored warnings from his own supporters.

**Evaluation and conclusion.** Without James's romanisation policies there would probably have been no revolution: the Tories, bishops and gentry would have stayed loyal and William would have had no support. However, the revolution was also about the constitution, and William's military intervention and the Catholic heir were decisive immediate causes. To a very large extent, therefore, the Catholic policies of James II explain the revolution, but they influenced it together with fears of absolutism and the European dimension of William's invasion.
